overview.title: 📖 Overview: Closing the Chapter on Doubtful Sins
overview.subtitle: Keritot 23a–23b
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf works through the mishna's full grid of two-piece scenarios — forbidden fat paired with non-sacred meat, consecrated food, sacrificial forbidden fat, or notar — tracking exactly which offerings one or two people owe in each combination, and testing whether Rabbi Shimon's rulings are internally consistent regarding whether one prohibition can take effect atop another. The Gemara concludes that sacrificial food is a unique case where the Torah does allow layered prohibitions, unlike ordinary non-sacred items. The chapter then closes, and a new mishna opens: what happens to an animal already designated as a provisional guilt offering when it becomes known that no sin was ever committed — compared point by point with a definite guilt offering, an ox sentenced to stoning, and the decapitated heifer of an unsolved murder, each handled differently depending on exactly which stage of its process had been reached.

slides.title: 🥩 The Escalating Piece-Combinations
slides.subtitle: The mishna's full grid of two-piece uncertainty scenarios
rows: Sin offering (certain fat was eaten); + provisional guilt offering per Rabbi Akiva
Two sin offerings + definite guilt offering
Forbidden fat + forbidden fat that is notar
Three sin offerings (two for fat, one for notar)

callout.label: Two-people variant:
callout.text: When two different people each eat one piece, Rabbi Akiva has each bring his own provisional offering; Rabbi Shimon has them jointly bring ONE definite offering as partners (stipulating whoever is liable receives it); Rabbi Yosei denies two people can ever jointly bring one offering at all.

slides.title: 🐖 Does Notar's Prohibition 'Land' on Already-Forbidden Fat?
slides.subtitle: Testing whether Rabbi Shimon consistently rejects layered prohibitions

lines.speaker: Rava
lines.text: Rabbi Shimon rules THREE sin offerings for forbidden fat that is also notar — meaning the notar prohibition takes effect even though the fat prohibition already applied. But doesn't Rabbi Shimon elsewhere reject this? He exempts one who eats neveila on Yom Kippur, since the neveila prohibition already covers the meat!

lines.speaker: First attempt
lines.text: Perhaps notar (a SEVERE prohibition) can land on the fat's prohibition, even though Yom Kippur's SEVERE prohibition can't land on neveila's LENIENT one — severity determines direction.

lines.speaker: Rejected
lines.text: That can't be right — neveila is lenient (lashes only) and Yom Kippur is severe (karet), yet the severe one still doesn't land on the lenient one. The pattern doesn't hold.

lines.speaker: Resolution
lines.text: Rather: specifically for SACRIFICIAL food, the Torah reveals that prohibitions DO stack — proven from the impurity prohibition landing on sacrificial portions already forbidden by both the 'ascend to the altar' rule AND the forbidden-fat prohibition (Lev. 7:20, 'which belong to the Lord').

callout.label: A parallel proof:
callout.text: Rebbi similarly holds that misuse of consecrated property (a lenient, death-at-Heaven's-hand prohibition) lands atop the SEVERE forbidden-fat prohibition specifically for offerings — confirming sacrificial food is genuinely exceptional.

slides.title: 💰 Why Doesn't Spoiled Notar Need a Guilt Offering Too?
slides.subtitle: If notar is sacrificial food, shouldn't eating it also trigger misuse liability?

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rava's question: notar is sacrificial food — so eating it should ALSO require a definite guilt offering for misuse, alongside the three sin offerings
2️⃣ Rav Naḥman's answer: this particular case involves notar worth LESS than a peruta — no misuse liability applies below that threshold
3️⃣ Challenge: but the mishna's OWN earlier clause (fat + sacrificial fat) explicitly requires a peruta's worth to generate a definite guilt offering — so why treat notar differently?

4️⃣ Resolved: notar specifically has lost value through spoilage — by the time it's notar, most people wouldn't pay for it. Two further explanations offered: a SMALL piece of notar vs. a LARGE one, or notar in SUMMER (spoils fast) vs. WINTER (stays edible longer)

callout.label: Why it matters:
callout.text: This resolves an apparent inconsistency between different clauses of the same mishna by locating a genuine factual difference in the value of the food involved.

slides.title: 🐑 What Happens to a Discovered-Innocent Guilt Offering?
slides.subtitle: A new mishna compares four cases where a designated offering turns out to be unnecessary

boxes.title: Provisional guilt offering
items: Before slaughter: R' Meir — released to graze (never truly consecrated); Rabbis — stays consecrated (must become blemished, then sold); R' Eliezer — sacrifice it anyway, it may cover an UNKNOWN sin
After slaughter: blood poured out, meat burned
After blood sprinkled: meat may be eaten (R' Yosei extends this even to blood still in the cup)

boxes.title: Definite guilt offering, stoned ox, decapitated heifer
items: Definite guilt offering: before slaughter, released to graze; after slaughter, buried (never eaten, unlike provisional); after blood sprinkled, still burned, not eaten
Stoned ox: once actually stoned, benefit becomes PERMITTED regardless of later exoneration
Decapitated heifer: once its neck is broken, it's buried in place — its purpose (atoning for the uncertainty) is already fulfilled and cannot be undone

callout.label: The pattern across all four:
callout.text: Each case is judged by whether its defining ritual act (slaughter, stoning, decapitation) has already occurred — before that point, discovery of the truth cancels everything; after it, the act's consequences are generally locked in, though exactly how differs case by case.

slides.title: ❤️ Why Do Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis Disagree?
slides.subtitle: The philosophical root of the provisional-guilt-offering dispute

lines.speaker: Rabbi Meir
lines.text: Since it turns out he never needed this animal, its consecration is retroactively nullified — as though it was never sanctified at all.

lines.speaker: The Rabbis
lines.text: No — at the moment he consecrated it, his conscience was genuinely troubled by uncertainty. That sincere resolve to consecrate stands, regardless of what's later discovered.

lines.speaker: A Sage's clarification
lines.text: This dispute applies in BOTH directions: even when it turns out he DID sin (needing an ordinary sin offering instead), Rabbi Meir still releases the provisional animal to graze — since at the moment of consecration, he didn't yet KNOW he had sinned.

lines.speaker: Symmetric case
lines.text: And even when it turns out he did NOT sin, the Rabbis still hold the animal consecrated — since his pangs of conscience at the time were real, independent of the eventual outcome.

callout.label: Underlying question:
callout.text: Does consecration depend on the objective facts turning out to justify it, or on the subjective sincerity of the person's state of mind at the moment he acted?

summary.principle: The mishna's detailed grid of two-piece uncertainty cases, together with the closing rules for a mistakenly-consecrated offering, together demonstrate that halakhic outcomes track precise factual distinctions — value thresholds, the special status of sacrificial food, and the exact ritual stage reached — rather than any single blanket rule.

flowSteps.content: 🥩 The mishna maps every combination of forbidden fat with chullin, hekdesh, and notar to its precise required offerings
🐖 Rabbi Shimon's rulings on layered prohibitions are tested and found consistent — sacrificial food is a genuine Torah-revealed exception
💰 Spoiled notar's reduced value explains why it doesn't also trigger a misuse guilt offering

columns.content: 🐑 A discovered-innocent offering is judged by exactly which ritual stage it had reached
❤️ Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis disagree on whether sincerity or eventual fact determines an offering's validity

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: halakhic consequences are always anchored to precise facts — value, category, and procedural stage — never to a sweeping generalization

quiz.q: According to the mishna, what offering(s) does one bring after eating a piece of forbidden fat followed by a piece of sacrificial permitted fat, when he doesn't know which piece he ate first?
o: Nothing at all
A provisional guilt offering after the first piece, then a sin offering and a definite guilt offering for misuse after eating the second piece too
Only a sin offering
Only a definite guilt offering
quiz.e: The mishna rules that after the first piece (uncertain), he brings a provisional guilt offering; once he eats the second piece too, he certainly ate both the forbidden fat and the sacrificial fat, requiring a sin offering plus a definite guilt offering for misuse.

quiz.q: According to the Gemara's resolution, why can Rabbi Shimon hold that the notar prohibition takes effect atop the already-existing forbidden-fat prohibition, when he elsewhere holds that Yom Kippur's prohibition does NOT take effect atop a neveila's prohibition?
o: Because notar is always more severe than any other prohibition
Because specifically with regard to sacrificial food, the Torah reveals that prohibitions do take effect atop one another, unlike with non-sacred food
Because Rabbi Shimon actually contradicts himself with no resolution
Because neveila and notar are the same prohibition
quiz.e: The Gemara resolves this by showing that sacrificial food is a special case where the Torah explicitly allows layered prohibitions (proven from the impurity prohibition applying to already-forbidden sacrificial portions), unlike ordinary non-sacred food.

quiz.q: According to Rav Naḥman, why doesn't eating notar (which is sacrificial food) also trigger a definite guilt offering for misuse of consecrated property in this mishna's case?
o: Because notar is never actually sacrificial food
Because this notar, having spoiled, is worth less than a peruta — the minimum value required for misuse liability
Because misuse liability never applies to notar under any circumstances
Because the person already brought enough offerings
quiz.e: Rav Naḥman explains that spoiled notar has lost enough value that it falls below the peruta threshold required for misuse liability, distinguishing it from the earlier clause involving fresh sacrificial fat.

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, what happens to a provisional guilt offering (per the Rabbis' view) if it becomes known BEFORE slaughter that the person never sinned?
o: It is immediately released to graze as a non-sacred animal
It retains its consecrated status as a disqualified offering — it must graze until blemished, then be sold, with proceeds going to communal gift offerings
It is sacrificed anyway
It is buried immediately
quiz.e: The Rabbis (unlike Rabbi Meir) hold that the animal's consecration stands, since the owner's sincere concern at the time of designation was real; it becomes a disqualified offering that must graze until blemished before being sold.

quiz.q: According to the mishna, what is unique about an ox sentenced to be stoned, compared to a provisional guilt offering, once the defining act (stoning) has already occurred and the ox is later found innocent?
o: It must still be buried like the guilt offering
Deriving benefit from its carcass becomes permitted, since its stoned status is fixed regardless of the later discovery
It is treated exactly like the provisional guilt offering
Nothing changes about its status
quiz.e: The mishna teaches that once the ox has actually been stoned, benefiting from its carcass becomes permitted — the outcome is locked in by the completed act, distinguishing it from the provisional guilt offering's more flexible rules before its blood is sprinkled.
